newsitem.title: USA: U.S. aluminum premiums spurred by stranded cargoes.
newsitem.headline: U.S. aluminum premiums spurred by stranded cargoes.

text.p: U.S. aluminum premiums have firmed to 6.50 to 7.00 cents a pound over LME cash on metal delivered in March as physical tightness is compounded by metal laden barges being stranded in the cresting Ohio River, traders said.
"Make hay while the sun shines," a dealer with metal available said. "If you can deliver next week then maybe you can get 7.25 cents."
But another dealer cautioned, "We feel it's starting to peak around here."
Merchants estimated that 20,000 to 30,000 tonnes of primarily A7E Russian metal en route from LME warehouses in Europe to customers in the U.S. are trapped on barges in the flooded Ohio.
Some traders are scrambling for alternative supplies as they watch sunken piers make unloading impossible.
"It was destined to reach customers in the first half of March, but now it will be late March arriving," a dealer said. "In the interim we are seeing a second wave of emergency type buying."
No short-term relief is seen from the U.S. mills.
U.S. producers were already said to be short before the flooding occured as they bought metal on the open market to feed their fabrication plants.

But traders said the high premiums were only on very prompt metal, and soon dipped on shipments further forward. The nearby deals were for small amounts, 100 to 200 tonnes, just what customers needed to tide them over.
More metal from LME depots in Europe has been loaded and floated and, as yet, much of it is still unsold, traders said.
But if premiums are peaking at current levels, buyers will be wary of paying 6.5 to 7.0 cents now if premiums will be lower when the material arrives in the U.S.
"I certainly believe that, at this point, if somebody needs something next week, they could be paying close to 8.0 cents," a Midwest aluminum official said.
Some dealers were beginning to ask if aluminum production in the region was being affected because alumina and coke is shipped up river to plants such as Alcan's Sebree smelter in Kentucky.
"The facility itself has more than enough (raw material) inventory to see it through any forseeable closure of the river," said Alcan spokesman Charles Belbin. "It's not a concern."
Most of the metal produced at Sebree is trucked out.

Alcoa's Warrick smelter and fabricating plant is located on the Ohio, and plant official Mike Belwood, said deliveries of alumina and coal by barge have been disrupted because the unloading facility is under water.
"(But) The plant itself is above the flood level and we have sufficient inventories. We are humming along very well right now," Belwood said.
Traders said prices of pure grade aluminum scrap were also rising because some customers could not get enough prime metal.
